slides.0.title: Regulation in depth and reading the label
slides.0.subtitle: From codes and sweetness terms to name protection
slides.1.title: What every label must show
slides.1.highlights.0.title: Name and producer
slides.1.highlights.0.content: Under the DGCCRF guide the sales name “Champagne” must appear in very prominent characters, with the name or trade name of the maker (élaborateur) and the commune of its head office
slides.1.highlights.1.title: Sugar-level term
slides.1.highlights.1.content: It must be one of: brut nature, extra brut, brut, extra sec, sec, demi-sec or doux — the seven legal terms, with no room for invented words such as “very dry”
slides.1.highlights.2.title: Professional registration number
slides.1.highlights.2.content: Issued by the Comité Champagne and preceded by the initials of the maker’s category (NM, RM, CM and so on) — the “NM-123-456” a consumer sees in small print
slides.1.highlights.3.title: Other mandatory items
slides.1.highlights.3.content: Origin (Produit de France or equivalent), actual alcohol strength, nominal volume, lot number, allergens and the pregnancy warning (message or logo) (DGCCRF). Labelling rules are revised over time, so check current regulation
slides.1.content: Separate “must have” from “optional”: Blanc de Blancs, Millésime and Grand Cru are optional additions, but once written they are bound by the rules.
slides.2.title: The full code table: NM, RM, CM, RC, SR, ND, MA
slides.2.highlights.0.title: NM and CM
slides.2.highlights.0.content: NM (négociant-manipulant) buys grapes, must or wine and completes at least the final stages in its own premises; the large houses fall here. CM (coopérative de manipulation) is a cooperative making wine from its members’ grapes in its own premises (DGCCRF)
slides.2.highlights.1.title: RM and RC
slides.2.highlights.1.content: RM (récoltant-manipulant) makes only wine from its own harvest on its own premises. RC (récoltant-coopérateur) delivers grapes to a cooperative and takes back wine in progress or ready to sell, marketing it under its own name (DGCCRF)
slides.2.highlights.2.title: ND and MA
slides.2.highlights.2.content: ND (négociant distributeur) buys finished bottles and applies its own labelling; MA (marque d’acheteur) is a finished bottle dressed under the customer’s brand, for example a restaurant, supermarket or merchant own-label (DGCCRF, Glass of Bubbly)
slides.2.highlights.3.title: SR and “not a quality grade”
slides.2.highlights.3.content: SR (société de récoltants) is several growers sharing a winery, keeping their grapes separate and selling under their own brands (Glass of Bubbly; the DGCCRF page does not list this code). The DGCCRF stresses that a code says nothing about quality: RM is not automatically better than NM, only a different business model
slides.2.content: The code says who made it and who sells it, not how good it is. When using codes to infer style, speak of tendencies, not certainties.
slides.3.title: Vintage, variety and village: conditions for claims
slides.3.highlights.0.title: Millésime: the grapes must come from that year
slides.3.highlights.0.content: DGCCRF: a vintage may be declared only if the single year’s wine is judged remarkable, and then 100% of the grapes must come from that year (85% under the general rules). This is different from the Level 2 rule that vintage wine may not exceed 80% of that year’s output and may contain no reserve wine: one is “composition in the bottle”, the other “quota for the year”
slides.3.highlights.1.title: Single variety and Blanc de Blancs/Noirs
slides.3.highlights.1.content: If only one variety is claimed, 100% of the grapes must be that variety (85% under general rules); Blanc de blancs is white grapes only, Blanc de noirs black grapes only, and Rosé may come from blending or saignée (DGCCRF). These are optional additions
slides.3.highlights.2.title: Grand Cru, Premier Cru and village names
slides.3.highlights.2.content: Only villages on the specification’s list may use Grand or Premier Cru: 17 Grand Cru and 42 Premier-Cru-only (INAO 2024; the 42/44 discrepancy is in Level 2). Stating a village or lieu-dit requires all base-wine grapes to come from it, and a village off the list must be preceded by “Vigne de” or “Vignoble de” (Level 2)
slides.3.highlights.3.title: Prestige / Cuvée Spéciale
slides.3.highlights.3.content: “Prestige cuvée”, “Tête de cuvée” and the like are market terms with no legal definition in the INAO specification or the DGCCRF guide (Level 2). When reading a label go back to objective data: vintage, ageing, cru, dosage and disgorgement date, not the name itself
slides.3.content: Keep the two 100%s apart: Millésime (100% from that year) and single variety (100% of that variety); both are stricter than the 85% of the general rules.
slides.4.title: Name protection and the Comité Champagne
slides.4.highlights.0.title: “Champagne” is a protected designation
slides.4.highlights.0.content: At EU level Champagne is a protected geographical name reserved for sparkling wine meeting the AOC specification; other regions using the same method cannot borrow it. Protection varies by country, and individual cases (for example semi-generic use in some markets) should be checked against local law; this lesson does not list them country by country
slides.4.highlights.1.title: The ban on “méthode champenoise”
slides.4.highlights.1.content: Cellars (2025) says EU rules have barred non-Champagne regions from using “Méthode Champenoise” since 1994, so producers elsewhere switched to “traditional method” or terms such as Crémant. The year is a single-source statement; for the exam just remember that within the EU the phrase is reserved for Champagne and others say traditional method (méthode traditionnelle)
slides.4.highlights.2.title: The role of the Comité Champagne
slides.4.highlights.2.content: An interprofessional body created by the law of 12 April 1941, made up of the growers’ SGV and the houses’ UMC (Level 2). Its tasks include setting the yearly marketable yield, issuing professional registration numbers, compiling statistics and promotion; defending the Champagne name is part of its mission (individual legal cases not verified)
slides.4.highlights.3.title: Practice: decode a fictional label
slides.4.highlights.3.content: Example (fictional): “Champagne · Extra Brut · Blanc de Blancs · Millésime 2015 · NM-000-000”. Reading: 0–6 g/L sugar; white grapes only; 100% of the grapes from 2015; NM = a house that buys grapes; you still need the disgorgement date and time on lees to judge the style
slides.4.content: MW questions often use regulation as evidence: the price of a protected name is that producers accept strict specifications and yield management.
slides.5.componentProps.slide.title: 🧠 Knowledge check
What does the label code “RM” mean?
A. négociant-manipulant: a house that buys grapes
B. coopérative de manipulation: a cooperative
C. marque d’acheteur: a buyer’s own brand
D. récoltant-manipulant: makes only wine from its own harvest on its own premises
DGCCRF: RM makes only its own harvest; NM is a house, CM a cooperative and MA a buyer’s brand.
Under the DGCCRF guide, what share of the grapes must come from the year when a Millésime is stated?
100% from that year (85% is the general rule); 80% is the cap on vintage wine as a share of that year’s wine, a separate rule.
Which statement about “Prestige cuvée” is correct?
A. It must be made from Grand Cru grapes
B. It must be aged at least ten years
C. A market term with no legal definition in the INAO specification or the DGCCRF guide
D. It must be Brut Nature
Prestige is the market name for a house’s flagship; the specification defines nothing and sets no minimum ageing or cru requirement.
